To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
immune complexes bound to CR1 on red blood cells can be transferred between red blood cells and that this is dependent on the number of CR1 on both the donor and recipient cells.
the binding and release of immune complexes from erythrocytes is influenced by the number of CR1 molecules on the cell.
the rate of transfer of complement-opsonized immune complexes between red blood cells is related to the CR1 concentration of the donor and recipient cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of erythrocyte complement receptor type 1 (CR1) in the removal of immune complexes.
the role of erythrocyte complement receptors in the clearance of immune complexes from circulation.
the interaction of erythrocyte complement receptor type 1 and immune complexes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the CR1 on erythrocytes can act as a dynamic buffer system which prevents immune-complexes that have bound complement (C3) from binding to vascular endothelial cells and thereby causing damage.
erythrocyte C3b receptors are not involved in immune complex clearance, but are important for immune complex transfer.

the number of CR1 on a cell determines the rate at which C3b- and iC3B-opsonized immune complexes transfer from one erythrocytes to another, but not the rate at which immune complexes bind to the erythrocyte.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
erythrocytes with low numbers of CR1 are less efficient in the clearance of immune complexes, whereas erythrocytes of high CR1 numbers are more effective in the clearance of complexes.
erythrocytes with high CR1 number are more effective in binding and clearing immune complexes from the circulation than cells with low CR1.
CR1 on erythrocytes may act as a buffer for immune complexes, preventing them from being deposited on endothelial cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the CR1 numbers of donor and recipient cells are critical determinants of the transfer reaction.
CR1 is not a passive opsonin, but a highly regulated receptor that controls the transfer of C3b- and iC3B-opsonized immune complexes to erythroid cells.
the number of complement receptor type 1 (CR1) molecules on erythrocytes affects the binding and release of immune complexes.
